prompt: In many countries, companies are employing fewer permanent staff and are using more short-term contractors and gig workers. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Permanent employment is being replaced in many industries by short contracts, agency work and app-based freelancing. I regard this as a negative development overall, although my reasons have less to do with flexibility than with who now carries the cost of a bad month.

The advantages are genuine for a minority. A skilled contractor with sought-after expertise can charge more than a salaried equivalent, refuse work and take time off without asking permission. For students and for people with caring responsibilities, work that can be fitted around other commitments is often the only work available at all. Companies benefit too, since they can expand and contract quickly without the cost of redundancies, and in genuinely seasonal industries that is a reasonable arrangement rather than an abusive one.

The problem is that these conditions describe a small part of the workforce. Most gig work is low paid and easily replaced, which removes the bargaining power that made flexibility valuable in the first place. Sick pay, pensions, notice periods and holiday entitlement were never perks; they were the mechanism by which the risk of illness or a slow month sat with the employer, who could absorb it, rather than with the worker, who cannot. A salaried employee who catches flu loses nothing; a courier who catches flu loses a week of income. Reclassifying the same jobs shifts that risk downwards without changing the work at all.

This is why I consider the trend negative. Flexibility that one side can use and the other cannot is not flexibility but insecurity with a better name, and the shift has happened largely at the bottom of the labour market rather than at the top. The label has changed and the work has not.
title: Permanent jobs giving way to gig and contract work
